syllabus.clause: array-backed circular deque vs chunked block deque (C++ std::deque) and their iterator-stability trade-offs

at.step: Does a deque need two separate structures?
Does pushing onto a deque's front move anything?

items.item: insert/erase at either end is O(1); in the middle, linear
insertion at either end invalidates iterators but not references to surviving elements

at.step: Does pushing onto a deque's front move anything?

items.item: erasure's invalidation depends on which end is touched
VecDeque is a growable ring buffer; elements not necessarily contiguous
a stack restricts access to one end (push/pop both there); an undo history is a real use where the most recent action is undone first
a queue splits access across two ends; a task queue is a real use where the oldest waiting task runs first
a deque is one structure with O(1) push/pop/peek at both ends directly, not a composition of a stack and a queue

at.step: Does a deque need two separate structures?

items.item: a stack or a queue is a deque's interface used with a self-imposed restriction, not a structurally weaker data structure
an array-backed ring buffer resizes by reallocating, exactly like a dynamic array; a chunked block deque grows by adding a block without moving existing elements
Rust's VecDeque is a real, shipped example of the ring-buffer design, documented as such in its own words

std::deque's own invalidation rule is a specific split: insertion at either end invalidates iterators but not references to elements already present, the opposite of a vector's reallocation invalidating everything at once

at.step: Does pushing onto a deque's front move anything?

items.item: mixing up which of the two deque designs backs a piece of code is a real, sourced way to introduce a use-after-invalidation bug that only one of the two designs would actually produce

O(1) at both ends is a measurable property: a real ring-buffer-backed deque's per-operation cost stays flat from ten to ten thousand elements, while a plain list used the same way scales directly with size
the next topic builds a further invariant on top of a stack or queue, without changing which structure backs it
